question.text: What is the key difference between option premium calculation for equity options vs currency options?

answer.text: Equity options use one interest rate and dividend yield (Black-Scholes); currency options use two interest rates — domestic and foreign (Garman-Kohlhagen) — because both currencies earn interest
There is no difference — the same formula applies to both
Currency options are always cheaper because currencies are less volatile than stocks
Equity options use delta; currency options use a different Greek called 'phi'

explanation.text: The Logic: Equity option pricing typically uses a single risk-free interest rate and an adjustment for dividend yield (the Black-Scholes framework). Currency option pricing, in its standard form, must incorporate two interest rates — the domestic and the foreign rate — because both currencies in the pair earn interest. In the Garman-Kohlhagen formulation the foreign rate effectively plays the role of a continuous dividend yield on the spot exchange rate. The Trap: The equity and currency models are structurally similar but the inputs differ — they are not literally the same formula. Whether currency premiums end up cheaper or more expensive than equity premiums depends on volatility and rates, not on currencies being inherently less volatile. And both equity and currency options use the same standard Greeks, not a special "phi". Note: The NISM Series I (Currency Derivatives) workbook page reviewed states that Indian exchanges use the Black-Scholes model for currency options, and the Series VIII workbook covers equity option pricing, but the specific Garman-Kohlhagen two-interest-rate currency-option formula contrasting domestic and foreign rates against equity Black-Scholes was not located in the workbook pages reviewed. The framing above is presented as general option-pricing-theory industry knowledge rather than a workbook citation.
